The manual opens with the human cost: impaired driving is behind thousands of lives cut short, injuries and shattered families, and every impaired driver endangers everyone on the road. Young drivers are over-represented among impaired drivers in fatal crashes, which is one reason the penalties for young people are tougher. The manual also stresses that penalties are severe, that capture is likely, and that plea bargains are tightly limited. In this first lesson we look at how alcohol and drugs actually change the way a person drives.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What alcohol does","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slows reactions, dims vision.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},{"text":"Warps speed and distance sense.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},{"text":"Loosens inhibition, invites chances.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Alcohol slows your reactions and dims your vision. It warps your sense of speed and distance. It loosens your inhibitions and makes you more willing to take chances. It makes night driving deadlier, because glare from oncoming lights blinds you more easily. And it does all this from the first drink, before you look or feel drunk, while giving you false confidence that you are fine to drive. The manual points out that driving involves hundreds of decisions every mile, and alcohol corrupts them, as in the gamble a driver takes at a stop sign.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Drugs and mixtures","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drugs impair driving too.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Including some prescriptions and cannabis.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Mixing is far worse.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Driving impaired by drugs, by alcohol, or by a mix of the two is a crime. The drugs the manual names include marijuana and cannabis, cocaine, LSD, heroin, opium and some prescription medicines. Drugs degrade reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness, and they bring other dangers as well. Combined doses, such as alcohol together with a drug, severely wreck driving ability, and can damage health up to the point of death. So the question is not only whether you have been drinking, but whether anything you have taken could impair your driving.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Feeling fine is not proof","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alcohol acts from the first drink.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},{"text":"It breeds false confidence.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Looking sober is not being sober.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people judge whether they can drive by how they feel. The manual warns that alcohol acts from the first drink, before any drunk look or feel, and that it breeds false confidence about fitness. So feeling fine is exactly what alcohol tends to make you believe, even as your reactions slow and your judgment slips. The same goes for drugs, including some prescriptions, which can impair you without your noticing. The safe rule is to decide before you drink or take anything how you will get home, rather than trusting how you feel afterward.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the prescription rule","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"A prescription that impairs.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Is driving on it a crime?","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: is it a crime to drive while impaired by a prescription drug? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. Driving impaired by drugs, alcohol or their mix is criminal, and the drugs the manual names include some prescriptions, along with marijuana and cannabis, cocaine, LSD, heroin and opium. Drugs degrade reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness, and combining them with alcohol severely wrecks driving and can harm health up to death. So a valid prescription does not make impaired driving legal or safe.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Impairment in short","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every impaired driver endangers the road.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Alcohol acts from the first drink.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},{"text":"Drugs and mixtures impair too.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, impaired driving is behind lives cut short, injuries and shattered families, every impaired driver endangers the road, young drivers are over-represented in impaired fatal crashes, and penalties are severe with likely capture and tight plea-bargain limits. Alcohol slows reactions, dims vision, warps speed and distance sense, loosens inhibition, worsens night glare, and acts from the first drink while breeding false confidence. Driving impaired by drugs, alcohol or their mix is criminal, and mixing them is especially dangerous. Next we look at the offenses and blood alcohol testing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the impaired-driving offenses and how they are proved. The manual lists the offenses you can be arrested for, from alcohol impairment up to aggravated driving while intoxicated, and ties them to blood alcohol levels measured in breath, blood, urine or saliva. It explains that a driver can be convicted even without a chemical test, what happens to the license at sentencing, and how chemical testing works under implied consent. Finally, it explains why refusing a test is punished on its own track. We will build the offense ladder first, then turn to testing and refusal.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The arrestable offenses","fact_ids":["sec09-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Aggravated DWI, DWI, point-zero-eight-plus.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Drug, alcohol and combined impairment.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Measured in breath, blood, urine or saliva.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"The arrestable offenses are aggravated driving while intoxicated, driving while intoxicated, driving with a blood alcohol content of point-zero-eight or more, impairment by drugs, impairment by alcohol, and impairment by a combination. Blood alcohol can be measured in breath, blood, urine or saliva. A reading over point-zero-five counts as evidence of impairment. Point-zero-eight or more counts as evidence of intoxication. And point-one-eight or more counts as aggravated intoxication. So the number on the test does a lot of work: it helps decide which offense the driver is charged with.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Three rungs, three names","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Over point-zero-five: impairment.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Point-zero-eight: intoxication.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Point-one-eight: aggravated.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. People blur the offenses together as drunk driving. The manual separates them. Impairment covers alcohol, drugs or both. Intoxication needs point-zero-eight blood alcohol or drug-driven inability. Aggravated intoxication needs point-one-eight. Three rungs of one ladder. And the evidence levels follow the same pattern: over point-zero-five evidences impairment, point-zero-eight-plus evidences intoxication, and point-one-eight-plus evidences aggravation, so each decimal jump renames the crime. Learn the three numbers in order, and the name that goes with each one.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":32,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Convictions and the license","fact_ids":["sec09-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Officer testimony can convict.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05"]},{"text":"No chemical test needed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05"]},{"text":"License revoked or suspended at sentencing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"A driver can be convicted of impaired driving on an officer's testimony about the driving, appearance and behavior, without any chemical test at all. If the verdict is guilty, the court revokes or suspends the license at sentencing, and the license is taken at once. Commercial drivers face even tougher standards, which are covered in the commercial manual. So refusing or avoiding a test does not mean a conviction cannot happen. An officer's observations can be enough, and the license loss starts as soon as the sentence is imposed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Implied consent and refusal","fact_ids":["sec09-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driving grants consent to testing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Tests follow arrest.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Refusal: suspension, then hearing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"By driving in the state, you have already given consent to a chemical test of your blood, breath, urine or saliva after an arrest. This is called implied consent. Refusing the test is handled separately from the charge itself. Refusal brings a suspension at arraignment, it can be used as evidence at trial, and it can lead to revocation after a hearing confirms it, even if you are later acquitted of the impaired-driving charge. The penalties for refusal are detailed in the chapter on keeping your license. So refusal is never a clean way out.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Refusal stands apart","fact_ids":["sec09-R04","sec09-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Suspended at arraignment.","fact_ids":["sec09-R04","sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Revoked after a hearing.","fact_ids":["sec09-R04","sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Even if acquitted.","fact_ids":["sec09-R04","sec09-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a second trap. Some drivers think that if they refuse the test and are later found not guilty, nothing will happen to their license. The manual says refusing the chemical test suspends at arraignment and can revoke after a hearing even when the underlying charge acquits, punishment fully detached from guilt. So the refusal is its own problem, separate from whether you were impaired. An acquittal on the driving charge does not undo it. That is why the manual treats refusal as a choice with its own serious cost, rather than a shield against the charge.","fact_ids":["sec09-R04","sec09-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the levels","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R02","sec09-R01","sec09-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"A blood alcohol reading.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R02","sec09-R01","sec09-F05"]},{"text":"Which level is intoxication?","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R02","sec09-R01","sec09-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: what blood alcohol level counts as evidence of intoxication? Work it out before reading on. The answer is point-zero-eight or more. A reading over point-zero-five counts as evidence of impairment, and point-one-eight or more counts as aggravated intoxication. Remember the ladder: impairment, then intoxication, then aggravated intoxication, with each decimal jump renaming the crime. And remember that a chemical test is not the only route to conviction, because an officer's testimony about driving, appearance and behavior can convict without one.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R02","sec09-R01","sec09-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Offenses in short","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F05","sec09-F08","sec09-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Three levels name three offenses.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F05","sec09-F08","sec09-R04"]},{"text":"Testimony can convict.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F05","sec09-F08","sec09-R04"]},{"text":"Refusal is punished on its own.","fact_ids":["sec09-F04","sec09-R01","sec09-R02","sec09-F05","sec09-F08","sec09-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, the arrestable offenses run from alcohol or drug impairment through intoxication to aggravated intoxication, with blood alcohol over point-zero-five evidencing impairment, point-zero-eight-plus intoxication, and point-one-eight-plus aggravation. Officer testimony can convict without a chemical test, and the license is revoked or suspended at sentencing. Driving grants implied consent to testing after arrest. Refusal suspends at arraignment, is admissible at trial, and can revoke after a hearing even after acquittal. safer.","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Inside blood alcohol","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"What raises it.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07"]},{"text":"What lowers it.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson explains how blood alcohol content rises and falls. The manual says what sets your blood alcohol level and what does not, shows that standard servings of different drinks contain the same amount of alcohol, and explains roughly how much one drink adds and how long it takes to clear. Then it addresses popular beliefs about sobering up, which turn out to be wrong. Understanding these facts helps you see why no amount of drinking is safe before driving, and why the only real answer is to wait, or better, to arrange a sober ride ahead of time.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What sets blood alcohol","fact_ids":["sec09-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Number of drinks, spacing, body weight.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06"]},{"text":"Not drink type, fitness or tolerance.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06"]},{"text":"Women process slower.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Your blood alcohol level depends on how many drinks you have, how close together you have them, and your body weight. It does not depend on the kind of drink, on how fit you are, or on how much you usually drink. One and a half ounces of liquor, five ounces of wine, twelve ounces of beer and twelve ounces of cooler all contain the same amount of alcohol, and none is safer than another. For a one-hundred-fifty-pound man, each drink raises blood alcohol by about point-zero-two, which clears in roughly an hour, while women process alcohol more slowly and reach higher levels.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"No drink is safer","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Equal alcohol per standard serving.","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]},{"text":"Liquor, wine, beer, cooler.","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]},{"text":"Count, spacing and weight decide.","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people believe beer or wine is a safer choice than liquor. The manual says liquor, wine, beer and cooler carry equal alcohol per standard serving, with none safer, and that content follows count, spacing and weight rather than drink style, fitness or tolerance. So switching drinks does not lower your blood alcohol. Neither does being fit or being used to drinking. What matters is how many standard drinks you have, how fast, and how much you weigh. A drink is a drink, whatever is in the glass.","fact_ids":["sec09-R05","sec09-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Only time sobers","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Nobody is immune.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Food only slows absorption.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Coffee, exercise, showers just fight sleep.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Weight shifts blood alcohol, but nobody is immune. More drinks per hour mean higher content and worse driving, and just a few drinks can reach an illegal level, with effects from the first. Food in your stomach only slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. The only thing that sobers you up is time passing. Coffee, exercise and cold showers do not lower blood alcohol. They just fight sleep, so you may feel more awake while still being impaired. That gap between feeling awake and being sober is part of what makes these myths dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Awake is not sober","fact_ids":["sec09-R06","sec09-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Food, coffee, exercise, showers.","fact_ids":["sec09-R06","sec09-F07"]},{"text":"None lowers blood alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec09-R06","sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Only elapsed time clears it.","fact_ids":["sec09-R06","sec09-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a second trap. People try coffee, a cold shower, exercise or food to sober up before driving. The manual says food, coffee, exercise and cold showers never lower blood alcohol however awake they leave the drinker, since only elapsed time clears content. So the person who drinks three cups of coffee may feel alert, but their blood alcohol is no lower than before. Only time brings it down. If you have been drinking, the choices are to wait long enough or to get a sober ride, not to try a quick fix that only changes how you feel.","fact_ids":["sec09-R06","sec09-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check drink equivalence","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-R05","sec09-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Five ounces of wine.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-R05","sec09-F07"]},{"text":"What holds the same alcohol?","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-R05","sec09-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: which holds the same amount of alcohol as five ounces of wine? Standard servings of all four carry equal alcohol, and none is safer. What sets your blood alcohol is how many drinks you have, how close together, and your body weight. And once alcohol is in your system, only time lowers it. Coffee, exercise and cold showers just fight sleep.
